mainTopic: Which waters make fish without סנפיר and קשקשת forbidden, the sources for permitting fish in vessels, and when small creatures in drinks become a forbidden שרץ
overview: This עמוד asks which waters the תורה means when it forbids fish without fins and scales. The גמרא reads the words 'in the waters... in the seas and in the rivers... in the waters' as a כלל ופרט וכלל. That method includes only waters like seas and rivers, meaning flowing water. So fish from trenches and channels are forbidden, and fish from pits, ditches and caves are permitted. The school of רבי ישמעאל reads the same words as רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה and reaches the same result. Under both readings, the word תאכלו shows that more than just vessels is permitted. מתתיה בר יהודה explains why: still water is like a vessel. Next, רב אחא and רבינא disagree about which verse is the stated source for permitting fish in vessels and which is only implied. Then רב הונא warns not to filter beer through straw at night, because a creature that leaves the liquid and falls back in becomes a forbidden שרץ. Clinging to a vessel's walls is normal growth and does not count as leaving, and רב חסדא brings a ברייתא supporting רב הונא. The עמוד ends as שמואל begins a ruling about a wormy cucumber, which continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Placing the detail between the two generalizations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets the two mentions of 'in the waters' around 'in the seas and in the rivers' and reads them as a כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Put the detail between them and expound them as a generalization, a detail, and a generalization. 'In the waters' is a generalization. 'In the seas and in the rivers' is a detail. 'In the waters' then generalizes again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the two general phrases 'in the waters' and puts the specific phrase 'in the seas and in the rivers' between them. This sets up the next step, where it uses the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this point, the two general phrases were sitting next to each other with no detail between them. By placing the פרט in the middle, the גמרא turns the verses into a standard כלל ופרט וכלל. Now a fixed rule of expounding can be used to decide which waters are included.

keyTerms.meaning: Place the detail between them (between the two generalizations)
A generalization: a broad phrase in a פסוק
A detail: a specific item listed in a פסוק
It went back and generalized again

phrases.english: Place the detail between them
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the two times the פסוקים say 'in the waters' (ויקרא 11:9-10).

phrases.english: and expound them as a generalization, a detail, and a generalization.
'In the waters' – it generalized;
'in the seas and in the rivers' – it specified;
'in the waters' – it went back and generalized.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַטֵּל פְּרָט בֵּינֵיהֶם וְדוּנֵם בִּכְלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion (before this section) about the two generalizations next to each other in the פסוקים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוקים are read as כלל ('in the waters'), פרט ('in the seas and in the rivers'), כלל ('in the waters').

steps.title: Only waters similar to seas and rivers: flowing water
steps.stepSummary: Under כלל ופרט וכלל only things like the פרט are included, and the shared quality of seas and rivers is that they are flowing water.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a generalization, a detail, and a generalization, you include only things similar to the detail. Just as the detail clearly means flowing water, so too all flowing water is included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל: we include only things that are like the detail. It says the common feature of seas and rivers is that they are flowing water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The final כלל widens the law past seas and rivers, and the פרט in the middle limits how far it widens. The test is 'flowing water', so any water source that flows counts like seas and rivers.

keyTerms.meaning: Generalization, detail, generalization: a rule of expounding that includes only things similar to the detail
Similar to the detail
Clearly stated, explicit
Flowing water, water that springs and moves

phrases.english: A generalization, a detail, and a generalization –

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט,
phrases.english: you include only what is similar to the detail.
Just as the detail clearly means flowing water,
so too all flowing water is included.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּלָל וּפְרָט וּכְלָל אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל to the structure set up in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The איסור covers fish found in any flowing water, similar to seas and rivers.

steps.title: What is included and what is excluded
steps.stepSummary: The 'flowing water' test includes trenches and channels as forbidden and leaves pits, ditches and caves as permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does it include? Trenches and channels, to forbid. And what does it exclude? Pits, ditches and caves, to permit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out what the 'flowing water' rule means in practice. It shows what the last כלל adds and what the פרט leaves out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trenches (חריצין) and channels (נעיצין) are not seas or rivers, but their water flows, so fish without fins and scales there are forbidden. Pits, ditches and caves hold still water, so they do not match the פרט, and fish found there are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it include? (what does the final generalization add)
What does it exclude?
Trenches and water channels: man-made paths where water flows
Pits, ditches, and caves: places holding still water
To forbid / to permit

steps.whatToRemember: With the 'flowing water' test, fish without fins and scales from trenches and channels are forbidden, and those from pits, ditches and caves are permitted.

phrases.english: What does it include?
Trenches and channels, to forbid.
And what does it exclude?
Pits, ditches, and caves, to permit.
phrases.notes: These hold still water, so fish without fins and scales found there are allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the practical results of the 'flowing water' test from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trenches and channels are forbidden; pits, ditches and caves are permitted.

steps.title: Why not a broader likeness: any water on the ground?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the shared feature could instead be 'water found on the ground', which would forbid even pits, ditches and caves and exclude only vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: just as the detail clearly means water found on the ground, so too all water found on the ground is included. What does it include? Even pits, ditches and caves, to forbid. And what does it exclude? It excludes vessels!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the choice of 'flowing water' as the shared feature. It suggests a wider feature, 'water on the ground', that would forbid almost everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Seas and rivers are flowing, but they are also water lying on the ground. If we pick that wider feature, pits, ditches and caves would match the פרט too and become forbidden. Only water in vessels would be left out, so the earlier result would be overturned.

keyTerms.meaning: But say instead (proposing another reading)
Water that 'grows' (is found) on the ground
Vessels, containers

steps.confusionAlert: 'Growing' water here does not mean water that gets bigger. It just means water that is naturally found on the ground, as opposed to water in a container.

phrases.english: But say: just as the detail clearly means
water that grows on the ground,
phrases.notes: 'Grows' here means 'is found': water lying in the ground, not in a container.

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל מַיִם גְּדֵלִין עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע.
phrases.english: so too all water that grows on the ground is included.
And what does it include?
Even pits, ditches, and caves, to forbid.
And what does it exclude? It excludes vessels!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: מָה הַפְּרָט מְפוֹרָשׁ מַיִם גְּדֵלִין עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'flowing water' test from steps 2-3 by proposing a broader shared feature.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice of 'flowing water' as the feature shared by seas and rivers.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Seas and rivers also share a broader feature, being water on the ground. Using that would forbid pits, ditches and caves and exclude only vessels.

steps.title: Then what would the word 'you may eat' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that if only vessels were excluded, the phrase 'these you may eat' would teach nothing, so the broad reading is rejected.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what use is the word 'you may eat'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a question. If only vessels were left out, the words 'these you may eat' would serve no purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vessels are nothing like seas and rivers, so they would be left out even without extra words. The phrase 'את זה תאכלו מכל אשר במים' must be teaching that more is permitted, namely pits, ditches and caves. So the narrower 'flowing water' test stands.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
What does it accomplish? What does it add?
You may eat (from the פסוק 'את זה תאכלו מכל אשר במים')

steps.whatToRemember: The word תאכלו shows that more than just vessels is permitted. So the test is 'flowing water': trenches and channels are forbidden, and pits, ditches and caves are permitted.

phrases.english: If so, 'you may eat' –
phrases.notes: From ויקרא 11:9: 'את זה תאכלו מכל אשר במים'.

phrases.english: what does it accomplish?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the broader reading of step 4 and supports the 'flowing water' reading of steps 2-3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the challenger's reading would leave a word of the פסוק with nothing to teach.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The shared feature is any water on the ground, so only vessels are excluded.
steps.terutzMaskana: תאכלו must permit something more, so the shared feature is flowing water, and pits, ditches and caves are permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a word in the פסוק must teach something, and that rule decides which likeness to the פרט we follow.

steps.title: The school of רבי ישמעאל reads the verse as amplify, restrict, amplify
steps.stepSummary: דבי רבי ישמעאל say the double 'in the waters' is not a כלל ופרט but a רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה, which includes everything except what the restriction leaves out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'In the waters' appears twice. This is not a general statement and a detail. It is an amplification and a restriction. 'In the waters' amplifies, 'in the seas and in the rivers' restricts, and 'in the waters' amplifies again. When a verse amplifies, restricts and amplifies again, it includes everything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second way of reading the same פסוק. The school of רבי ישמעאל uses the רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט method instead of כלל ופרט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under כלל ופרט וכלל, only things similar to the detail are included. Under רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה, almost everything is included, and only a small group is left out. The next steps show that, for these waters, the practical result still comes out the same.

keyTerms.meaning: An 'amplification and restriction': a method for reading a פסוק that includes widely
It went back and amplified again
It included everything, except what the restriction leaves out

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two methods. כלל ופרט וכלל includes only things that are like the detail. רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה includes almost everything.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two schools read the same words with different methods, so the boundaries of the איסור could change. The next steps check whether the practical result actually differs.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"In the waters," "in the waters" twice,
this is not a generalization and a detail,
rather, it amplified and restricted.
"In the waters": it amplified,
"in the seas and in the rivers": it restricted,
"in the waters": it went back and amplified.
Amplified, restricted, and amplified: it amplified everything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different method of reading the same פסוק that was read as כלל ופרט וכלל in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The double 'in the waters' is a רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה, which includes everything except a small excluded group.

steps.title: What is included and what is left out
steps.stepSummary: The amplification forbids fish in trenches and channels. The restriction permits fish in pits, ditches and caves.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did it include? Trenches and channels, to forbid them. And what did it leave out? Pits, ditches and caves, to permit them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה reading to real places where fish are found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being 'included' means being treated like seas and rivers, so fish there without fins and scales are forbidden. Being 'left out' means fish there are permitted. In practice, the result is the same as the 'flowing water' test from step 3.

keyTerms.meaning: Trenches (dug channels with water running through them)
Water channels
Pits, ditches and caves, where the water stands still
To forbid / to permit

phrases.english: What did it include?
Trenches and channels, to forbid;
and what did it exclude?
Pits, ditches and caves, to permit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the method from step 6 to specific bodies of water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fish without fins and scales in trenches and channels are forbidden. Those in pits, ditches and caves are permitted.

steps.title: Maybe only vessels are left out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the amplification should also forbid pits, ditches and caves, so that only vessels are left out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: What did it include? Pits, ditches and caves, to forbid them. And what did it leave out? Only vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back. If רִיבָּה הַכֹּל really means 'everything,' why not forbid even pits, ditches and caves?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge uses the wide nature of רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט וְרִיבָּה. Since this method includes almost everything, maybe the only thing left out is the smallest case, water in a vessel.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Say instead': it introduces another possible reading
Vessels or containers

phrases.english: Say instead:
What did it include?
Pits, ditches and caves, to forbid;
and what did it exclude? It excluded vessels.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא: מַאי רַבִּי? בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת לְאִיסּוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges where step 7 drew the line.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 7 that pits, ditches and caves are left out and permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רִיבָּה הַכֹּל suggests the widest inclusion, so perhaps only vessels are left out.

steps.title: Then 'you may eat' would teach nothing
steps.stepSummary: If only vessels were left out, the words 'these you may eat' would have no purpose, so pits, ditches and caves must be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what does the word 'you may eat' add?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with the same argument it used in step 5 for the other method.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vessels would be permitted even without a special word. The phrase 'these you may eat' must therefore permit something more, which is pits, ditches and caves.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: it introduces the problem that the suggestion would cause
What does it accomplish? (What would the word teach?)

steps.whatToRemember: Under both methods, the final result is the same. Trenches and channels are forbidden, while pits, ditches and caves are permitted.

phrases.english: If so,
what does "you may eat" accomplish for him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Avoiding an extra word: the suggested reading would leave a word with nothing to teach.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only vessels are left out, and pits, ditches and caves are forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'You may eat' permits pits, ditches and caves, so only trenches and channels are forbidden.

steps.title: Why not reverse it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: maybe pits, ditches and caves should be forbidden, and trenches and channels permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: But I could reverse it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again. Even if one group is forbidden and one is permitted, who says which one is which?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse does not say which group goes with seas and rivers and which goes with the permitted group. The challenge asks for a reason to choose this order.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I will reverse it': swap which case gets which ruling

phrases.english: But I can reverse it,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that there is one forbidden group and one permitted group, but questions which is which.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assignment in step 7 of which places are forbidden and which are permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Nothing in the verse decides the direction, so the opposite assignment seems just as possible.

steps.title: Still water is like a vessel
steps.stepSummary: מתתיה בר יהודה explains that pits, ditches and caves hold still water like vessels, so they are permitted like vessels. Trenches and channels flow, so they are not like vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: As מתתיה taught. מתתיה בר יהודה taught: Why did you choose to permit pits, ditches and caves and to forbid trenches and channels? I include pits, ditches and caves because their water is held in place like in vessels. I exclude trenches and channels because their water is not held in place like in vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'reverse it' challenge with a teaching of מתתיה בר יהודה, which gives a logical reason for the direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vessels are surely permitted. Pits, ditches and caves are the most similar to vessels because their water stays in one place. Trenches and channels have moving water, so they are more like rivers.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What did you see?': what is your reason for choosing this way?
To include / to exclude
Held in, still (water that does not flow)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the wording. Here 'include' means grouping a place together with vessels, so it is permitted. In step 7, 'include' meant grouping it with seas and rivers, so it was forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: The key difference is still water (like a vessel, permitted) versus flowing water (like a river, forbidden).

phrases.english: As Mattitya taught,
for Mattitya bar Yehuda taught:
What did you see
to include pits, ditches and caves, to permit,
and to exclude trenches and channels, to forbid?
I include pits, ditches and caves
which are held still like vessels,
and I exclude trenches and channels
which are not held still like vessels.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְתָנֵי מַתִּתְיָה, דְּתָנֵי מַתִּתְיָה בַּר יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the reversal challenge of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical similarity: each place is grouped with the case it most resembles.
steps.terutzMaskana: Still water is like a vessel and is permitted. Flowing water is like a river and is forbidden.

steps.title: Which verse is the unstated source and which is the stated source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which פסוק is the 'unstated' source and which is the 'stated' source for permitting fish in vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which one is the unstated source, and which one is the stated source?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It goes back to the ברייתא on the previous עמוד, which said that fish in vessels are permitted both in an unstated way and in a stated way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two פסוקים, one about fish that have fins and scales and one about fish that do not. The question is which of them openly teaches the היתר and which only hints at it.

keyTerms.meaning: Which one
Unstated, implied: taught only by inference
Stated outright, explicit

phrases.english: Which is the implicit and which is the explicit?
phrases.notes: This goes back to the ברייתא on the previous עמוד, which says vessels are permitted both in an unstated way and in a stated way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves away from the רִיבָּה וּמִיעֵט discussion to clarify a term in an earlier ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which of the two פסוקים is the stated source and which is the unstated source for permitting fish in vessels.

steps.title: רב אחא and רבינא disagree
steps.stepSummary: One says the 'has fins and scales' verse is the stated source and the 'has not' verse is unstated. The other says the opposite.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא and רבינא disagree about this. One says: the verse about fish that 'have' fins and scales is the stated one, and the verse about fish that 'have not' is the unstated one. The other says: the 'have not' verse is the stated one, and the 'have' verse is the unstated one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a מחלוקת between two אמוראים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both verses mention 'in the seas and in the rivers,' so each can show that vessels are different. The disagreement is only about which verse makes the היתר for vessels openly and which makes it by inference.

keyTerms.meaning: They disagree
'It has' (the verse about fish that have fins and scales)
'It has not' (the verse about fish without fins and scales)

steps.whatToRemember: Both אמוראים agree that fish in vessels are permitted. They only disagree about which verse is the open source.

phrases.english: Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about it:
One says:
"has" is the explicit one,
and "has not" is the implicit one,
and one says:
"has not" is the explicit one,
and "has" is the implicit one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It is a מחלוקת: one holds that 'has' is stated and 'has not' is unstated, and the other holds the reverse.

steps.title: Why the 'has fins and scales' verse is the stated source
steps.stepSummary: The view that the 'has fins and scales' verse is the stated source says that this is the verse vessels are actually learned from.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the one who says the 'has' verse is the stated source? He can tell you: it is from that verse that vessels are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning of the first opinion from Step 13 and gives his answer. He says the 'has fins and scales' verse is the one we actually learn the permission for vessels from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the previous עמוד, the permission for fish in vessels was learned from the 'has fins and scales' verse. So this opinion calls that verse the stated source, because the הלכה is read directly out of it.

keyTerms.meaning: Stated, explicit: the verse the law is openly learned from
They are permitted
Vessels, containers

phrases.english: What is the reason of the one who says
that the 'has' verse is the stated one?
He can say to you:
It is from it that vessels are permitted.
phrases.notes: This points back to the previous עמוד, where this פסוק was used to permit fish found in vessels.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר יֵשׁ לוֹ מְפוֹרָשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the first opinion presented in Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does this opinion call the 'has fins and scales' verse the stated source?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because the permission for vessels is drawn directly from that verse.

steps.title: Why the 'has not fins and scales' verse is the stated source
steps.stepSummary: The other view says the 'has not' verse is the stated source, because without it we would have read the 'has' verse the wrong way.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the one who says the 'has not' verse is the stated source? Because this verse proves how to read the other one. If we had only the other verse, I would have thought that in vessels, even a fish that has fins and scales may not be eaten.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reasoning of the second opinion. It says the 'has not' verse is what shows us how to understand the 'has' verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'has' verse alone could be read as: fish with fins and scales are allowed only when they are in seas and rivers, so in vessels even they would be forbidden. The 'has not' verse limits the ban to seas and rivers. That shows the place-limits are about the ban, so vessels are permitted. Since this verse settles the question, this opinion calls it the stated source.

keyTerms.meaning: Does not have: the verse about fish without fins and scales
It proves, it shows
I would have said: a mistaken first thought
Even though

steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions agree that fish in vessels are permitted. They only argue about which פסוק is the main source and which one just helps explain it.

phrases.english: What is the reason of the one who says
that the 'has not' verse is the stated one?
Because this one is what proves the meaning of that one,
for if we had only that one, I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: בְּכֵלִים, אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִית לֵיהּ –
phrases.english: in vessels, even though it has fins and scales,
you still may not eat it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר אֵין לוֹ מְפוֹרָשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning of the opposing opinion, completing the explanation of Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does this opinion call the 'has not' verse the stated source?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because it is needed to show that the 'has' verse permits vessels. Alone, the 'has' verse could have been read as forbidding even kosher fish found in vessels.

steps.title: Do not filter beer through straw at night
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that one should not filter beer through straw at night. A creature might crawl up onto the straw and fall back into the cup, and then it is a forbidden שרץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: A person should not filter beer through straw at night. Perhaps a creature will crawl out above the straw and then fall into the cup, and he will transgress 'the creeping thing that creeps on the earth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new practical ruling from רב הונא about tiny creatures in drinks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creature that grows in the liquid is permitted as long as it never left it. Once it crawls out onto the straw, it counts as a creature 'creeping on the earth' and becomes forbidden. If it then falls into the cup, the drinker cannot see this in the dark and may swallow it.

keyTerms.meaning: To filter, to strain
Beer
Straw, a bundle of twigs used as a filter
Night, evening
Separates, leaves the liquid
A creeping thing that creeps on the earth: the Torah's ban

steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not the beer itself. The problem is that the creature left the liquid and came back. Leaving the liquid is what turns it into a forbidden שרץ.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule that a creature that left its liquid and returned is forbidden. The next steps test exactly how far that idea goes.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
A person should not filter beer
through straw at night,
lest a creature crawl out above the straw
and then fall into the cup,
and he transgresses because of
phrases.notes: The printed גמרא has the word in round brackets; the corrected wording is the word in square brackets. The meaning is the same.

phrases.english: 'the creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: לָא לִשְׁפֵּי אִינָשׁ שִׁיכְרָא בְּצִבְיָיתָא בְּאוּרְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic connected to creatures that grow in liquids.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not filter beer through straw at night. A creature may leave the beer onto the straw, fall back into the cup, and be swallowed as a forbidden שרץ.

steps.title: The same worry should apply to the walls of any vessel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא: if crawling out and falling back is a concern, it should apply to any vessel, since a creature may climb the wall and fall back in.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then in a vessel too! Perhaps the creature crawls out onto the side of the vessel and then falls back into the vessel?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב הונא's worry by stretching it to every container of drink.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving the liquid for the straw makes the creature forbidden. So leaving the liquid for the vessel's wall should do the same. Then every drink in every cup would be a problem, which cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: introduces a challenge from the previous logic
Side wall
Vessel, container

phrases.english: If so, in a vessel too,
perhaps it crawls out onto the side of the vessel
and then falls back into the vessel?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's ruling in Step 16 by extending its logic.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's concern about a creature leaving the beer onto the straw
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If leaving the liquid makes it forbidden, climbing onto a vessel's wall should too. Then all drinks in vessels would be problematic.

steps.title: Clinging to the vessel's wall is normal growth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that sticking to the vessel's walls is the creature's normal way of growing, so it does not count as leaving the liquid.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, that is its normal growth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains that the walls of the vessel are different from the straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These creatures naturally grow along the sides of the container, so being on the wall is still part of their home in the liquid. The straw sticks up above the vessel, so crawling onto it really is leaving. That is why רב הונא's worry applies only to the straw.

keyTerms.meaning: There: in that case
Its growth, its natural way of growing

steps.whatToRemember: A creature that grew in a liquid becomes forbidden only if it truly leaves its place, like crawling onto straw above the vessel. Clinging to the vessel's own walls does not count as leaving.

phrases.english: There, that is its normal growth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 17 and defends רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases: the vessel's wall is the creature's natural place, but the straw is not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Climbing onto a vessel's wall is the same as climbing onto the straw, so all drinks should be a concern.
steps.terutzMaskana: The vessel's wall is where the creature normally grows, so it is not considered leaving the liquid. Only the straw creates the problem.

steps.title: A ברייתא permits drinking from pits, ditches, and caves
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source for the answer in step 18. It brings a ברייתא: one may drink straight from pits, ditches, and caves without worrying about the creatures in them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where do you see this? A ברייתא teaches: How do we know to include pits, ditches, and caves, so that a person may bend down and drink from them without holding back? The פסוק says: 'You may eat of all that are in the waters.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants a source for the idea that a creature clinging to the wall does not count as leaving the liquid. It brings a ברייתא about drinking from pits, ditches, and caves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the small creatures in pits, ditches, and caves are permitted, just like fish in the water. That alone does not prove the point yet. The next step will explain why this ברייתא proves the answer from step 18.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do you say this? (asking for a source)
Pits, ditches, and caves: water that sits in the ground
And he does not need to hold back
The פסוק teaches
To include

phrases.english: And from where do you say this?
As it is taught: From where do we include
pits, ditches, and caves,
that one may bend down and drink from them
and need not hold back?
The verse says:
"You may eat of all that are in the waters."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source for the answer given in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a creature clinging to its container's walls is normal growth and does not count as leaving the liquid.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that permits drinking directly from pits, ditches, and caves, based on 'You may eat of all that are in the waters.'

steps.title: Why the pits ברייתא proves the point
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: why doesn't the ברייתא worry that a creature crawled onto the side of the pit and fell back in? It must be because clinging to the side is the creature's normal growth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry that perhaps a creature crawled out onto the side and then fell back in! Rather, it must be that this is its normal way of growing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows exactly how the ברייתא proves the point. Since the ברייתא is not worried about creatures climbing the side of the pit, clinging to the side must not count as leaving the water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not a real attack. It is a way of showing why the ברייתא matters. If climbing the side counted as leaving the water, the ברייתא could not allow drinking freely. So the ברייתא must agree that clinging to the side is just the creature's normal growth.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us be concerned
It separated, meaning it crawled out
The side wall
Its normal way of growing

steps.confusionAlert: This question is not the גמרא doubting the ברייתא. The גמרא asks it so it can show that the ברייתא must agree with the answer from step 18.

phrases.english: But let us worry that perhaps
it crawled out onto the side
and then fell back in?
Rather, that is its normal way of growing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא פָּרֵישׁ לְדַפְנָא וַהֲדַר נָפֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא from step 19 proves the answer from step 18.
steps.raayaObject: Clinging to the walls does not count as leaving the liquid.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא does not worry about creatures on the sides of pits and caves, so climbing the sides must be normal growth.

steps.title: The same applies to beer in a vessel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא applies the lesson to the vessel case: here too, clinging to the vessel's wall is the creature's normal growth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, that is its normal way of growing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the proof back to the vessel from step 17. Just as in pits and caves, clinging to a vessel's wall is normal growth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the question from step 17. Any ordinary vessel is fine, because creatures that climb its walls never really left the liquid. Only filtering through straw creates the problem רב הונא was worried about.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too

steps.whatToRemember: A creature that clings to the walls of its container is still growing normally, so it stays permitted. It becomes a problem only when it truly leaves the liquid, as with straw used for filtering.

phrases.english: Here too,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the vessel of beer from step 17.

phrases.english: that is its normal way of growing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the proven rule from step 20 to the vessel case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Creatures clinging to a vessel's walls are growing normally and stay permitted. רב הונא's worry applies only to filtering through straw.

steps.title: רב חסדא brings a ברייתא supporting רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא tells רב הונא that a ברייתא supports him: gnats are forbidden only when the liquid was filtered. That means unfiltered gnats are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to רב הונא: There is a ברייתא that supports you. 'Every swarming thing that swarms on the earth' comes to include gnats that one filtered. The reason they are forbidden is that one filtered them. But if one did not filter them, they are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא brings a ברייתא that backs up רב הונא's ruling from step 16. The ברייתא forbids gnats only in liquid that was filtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When liquid is filtered, gnats can end up on the filter and fall back in. That counts as leaving the liquid, which is exactly רב הונא's worry about straw. Gnats in unfiltered liquid stay permitted even though they may cling to the walls, which also matches step 21.

keyTerms.meaning: That supports you
Gnats or tiny insects found in liquid
That one filtered
The reason is because of X, so without X it would be different (learning the reverse case)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that filtering is what turns permitted gnats into a forbidden שרץ. That is why רב הונא's warning about filtering is a real concern.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said to Rav Huna:
There is a baraita that supports you:
"Every swarming thing that swarms upon the earth"
comes to include gnats that one filtered.
The reason is because he filtered them;
but if he did not filter them, they are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives support from a ברייתא for רב הונא's ruling in step 16, which the גמרא has just finished defending.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's ruling that filtering creates a problem, while creatures that merely sit in a vessel are permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on 'כׇּל הַשֶּׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ עַל הָאָרֶץ' that forbids only filtered gnats. From this we learn that unfiltered gnats are permitted.

steps.title: שמואל begins a teaching about a wormy cucumber
steps.stepSummary: שמואל opens a new teaching about a cucumber that became infested with worms. His ruling continues in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: A cucumber that became wormy...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. This line sets up שמואל's ruling about worms that grew inside a cucumber, and the ruling itself comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic moves from creatures in liquid to creatures that grow inside fruits and vegetables. The question of whether such worms are forbidden will be settled in the continuation.

keyTerms.meaning: A cucumber
That became infested with worms

phrases.english: Shmuel said: A cucumber that became infested with worms

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching about creatures that grow inside produce.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is a cucumber that became wormy. The ruling continues beyond this text.
